summary: PASSporT defines a signed token that cryptographically vouches for the originator of a communication, such as a telephone number or a URI. It is built on JSON Web Token and is used as a building block for fighting caller ID spoofing in the STIR work.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a tamper-proof name tag for a phone call. If someone tries to change the name, the seal breaks and everyone can see it was faked.

how to sign a caller identity token

subtitle: A signed token that lets the receiving end check who a call or message claims to come from.

tldr.problem: Telephone networks let callers spoof the calling number, and bad actors use that for fraud. Receivers need a way to check an originating identity, even when the two ends have no direct trust relationship.
tldr.mechanism: PASSporT is a JSON Web Token with a fixed header and claims for the originating and destination identities and an issue time, signed with ES256 over a deterministic JSON form so the signature can be checked at the destination.
tldr.outcome: It gives signaling protocols a common, extensible way to sign originating identity. RFC 8224 uses it within SIP. It is not a complete answer on its own, since it is not full non-repudiation.

today: RFC 8225 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2018, and its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC points to RFC 8224 for its use within SIP.

sections.title: Why Signed Caller Identity
sections.content:
Modern telephone networks allow the calling party's number to be spoofed for many legitimate purposes, such as providing network features on behalf of a legitimate number. The RFC notes that bad actors have used the same ability for fraud, to trick people into believing the caller is someone they are not. It adds that the problem extends to many emerging forms of personal communications.

RFC 8225 defines the Personal Assertion Token (PASSporT): a method for creating and validating a token that cryptographically verifies an originating identity, or more generally a URI or telephone number representing the originator. The goal is a common framework for signing information about the originating identity in an extensible way, independent of any specific call logic.

How a token is transported in a given signaling protocol is intentionally out of scope. RFC 8224 covers the use of PASSporT within SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write any name on a letter. PASSporT adds a seal that only the real sender could make, so the receiver can tell if the name was faked.

sections.title: Built on JWT and JWS
sections.content:
PASSporT reuses the standard token formats JSON Web Token (JWT, RFC 7519) and JSON Web Signature (JWS, RFC 7515). JWT carries claims in JSON, which easily hold originating-identity information and are easy to extend. JWS provides a path for updating the cryptographic algorithms used for signatures.

The main value asserted is the originating identity, meaning the calling party or the initiator of a session. The signer does not have to be the originating identity. The token is created by an entity that is authoritative to assert the caller's identity, for example at a device that has authenticated with a user, or at a network entity with an authenticated trust relationship with that device.

The destination side needs to be able to verify the token and its signature. The certificate tied to the token is used to validate the signer's authority, generally through a certificate chain to the trust anchor for that application.
sections.plainLanguage: PASSporT does not invent a new kind of seal. It uses a seal format that already exists and just says what to write inside it.

sections.title: The PASSporT Header
sections.content:
The header is a JWS JOSE Header that says what the token is and how it was signed. It should include at least three parameters.

  • typ: MUST be the string passport.
  • alg: implementations MUST support ES256 and MAY support other algorithms from the JWA registry. Implementations using ES256 SHOULD use deterministic ECDSA if or when supported.
  • x5u: a URI pointing to the X.509 certificate or chain for the signing key, generally an HTTPS or DNSSEC resource with integrity protection.

The mandatory-to-support algorithm may be updated in future updates to the document, depending on cryptographic strength requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is the front of the envelope. It says what kind of token this is, which lock was used, and where to find the key to check it.

sections.title: The PASSporT Payload Claims
sections.content:
The payload holds the claims to be verified at the destination. Claim names MUST use ASCII, although claim values may contain other characters.

The iat (issued at) claim is required. It MUST indicate the date and time of the origination of the communication, in the NumericDate format. It helps protect against replay and cut-and-paste attacks.

Two further claims are required. orig MUST hold exactly one identity object, and dest MUST hold at least one, in an array. Each identity is either a telephone number (tn, canonicalized as in RFC 8224) or a URI (uri). If dest lists both, the tn array goes first, and the strings inside each array should be in lexicographical order. Other identity types could be added later through IANA-registered types.

An optional mky claim binds media keys to the signaled identity. It asserts the fingerprints carried in the SDP a=fingerprint attribute, as an array of objects with alg first and dig second, sorted by the concatenation of the alg and dig values. The dig value is the hexadecimal value without colons.
sections.plainLanguage: The payload is the note inside: who is calling, who is being called, and when. Only the note's exact words count, so everything has to be written the same careful way.

sections.title: Signing and Deterministic JSON
sections.content:
JSON can contain spaces and line breaks and lets keys appear in any order, so by itself it is non-deterministic. A signature only checks out if both ends compute exactly the same bytes. PASSporT therefore requires the JWS Protected Header and JWS Payload to be serialized by these rules, which are based on the JWK thumbprint rules of RFC 7638.

  • No whitespace or line breaks around any syntactic element.
  • Object keys ordered lexicographically by the Unicode code points of the member names.
  • JSON value literals lowercase.
  • Numbers encoded as integers unless the field says otherwise.
  • The rules apply recursively to member values and array values.

The signature is made as in JWS (RFC 7515, Section 5.1, Steps 1 through 6) and PASSporT MUST use the JWS Protected Header. Step 7, the JSON serialization, is not supported. Step 8 produces the final compact JWS form, which joins header, payload and signature with periods. Within extension claims, member names in one JSON object MUST NOT repeat, or serialization would not be deterministic.
sections.plainLanguage: To check a seal, both people must write the note with exactly the same spacing and the same order. The rules make sure everyone writes it the same way.

sections.title: The Compact Form
sections.content:
When the signaling protocol already carries the header and claim information, sending it again wastes bytes. The compact form leaves out the header and payload and keeps only the signature, written as two periods followed by the base64url-encoded signature: .. then the signature.

The destination then has to rebuild the header and claims in order to verify the signature. A protocol that uses the compact form MUST come with a specification of how to reconstruct them from its own signaling.

Even the full form should follow the same ordering and whitespace rules, in case a protocol needs to switch between full and compact forms without breaking the signature.
sections.plainLanguage: If both people already know what the note says, you can send just the seal and let the other person write out the note again to compare.

sections.title: Extending PASSporT
sections.content:
PASSporT carries only the minimum claims for securely asserting the originating identity. A using protocol can add more JWT claims, which are managed through the IANA JSON Web Token Claims registry. Implementations MUST support the baseline claims and MAY support extended ones.

If an extension needs the receiver to understand particular claims, it signals this with a ppt header parameter. Every ppt value must be defined in a specification that ties it to the required claims and behaviors. Relying parties MUST fail to validate a PASSporT with an unsupported ppt.

Extension rules: extensions MUST include the baseline claims, claims may only be appended and never removed or reordered, and the specification MUST say which claims it adds and in what order. A creator cannot assume the destination understands any extension. Compact form users MUST use only mandatory extensions signaled by ppt, and need a field to carry ppt, since the compact form omits the header.

IANA created a PASSporT Type registry for ppt values, with the policy Specification Required. The RFC also registers the application/passport media type and the claims orig, dest and mky.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add extra lines to the note. If the extra lines matter, you mark the envelope so a reader who does not understand them knows to refuse it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
To avoid replay and cut-and-paste attacks, PASSporTs SHOULD only be sent with application-level protocol information, such as a SIP INVITE, that matches the fields in the token. Two claims do the work. The iat value should be a reasonable time given clock drift and transmission time, and the dest value limits reuse of a valid token toward other destinations, so the destination should check that it matches the intended recipient.

The RFC also lists limits. The token should not be treated as a full solution for absolute non-repudiation. The signer and the end user may differ, and when a provider signs for a user, it MUST have an authenticated and secure relationship with that user or device. Applications should verify that the signer is authoritative, using an application-specific or service-specific set of common trust anchors.
sections.plainLanguage: The note says when it was written and who it is for. If someone copies it and sends it to a different person or much later, the receiver can see it does not fit.
